purpose.name: The Compass Rose
purpose.instructions: Combine gin, St-Germain, lemon juice, and bitters in a shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled. Strain into an ice-filled collins glass. Top with tonic water. Garnish with fresh thyme.
purpose.why: Elderflower and lavender quietly point you toward clarity, the way purpose often arrives—not as a shout, but a fragrance.

source.author: Adapted from classic gin fizz traditions
source.publication: The Savoy Cocktail Book by Harry Craddock

action.name: The Bitter Start
action.instructions: Stir all ingredients with ice in a mixing glass for 30 seconds. Strain into a chilled coupe or rocks glass with a large ice cube. Express orange peel over the drink and drop it in.
action.why: A Boulevardier—bold enough to get you off the couch. The bitterness is the point: it wakes you up.

learning.name: The Slow River
learning.instructions: Combine chamomile tea, honey syrup, and lemon juice in a glass with ice. Top with sparkling water. Stir gently. Garnish with a lemon wheel and mint sprig.
learning.why: Chamomile asks nothing of you. It simply invites you to sit, and in sitting, learn.

source.author: Inspired by traditional tisane pairings
source.publication: The Drunken Botanist by Amy Stewart

october.name: The Fallen Leaf
october.instructions: Stir all ingredients with ice for 30 seconds. Strain into a chilled coupe glass. Float a thin apple slice on top.
october.why: Calvados carries an orchard's worth of autumn in every sip—woodsmoke, bruised fruit, the last warm afternoon.

source.author: A variation on the classic Fallen Leaf cocktail
source.publication: The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks by David Embury

nostalgia.name: The Fireside
nostalgia.instructions: Gently warm apple cider with cinnamon, cloves, and star anise over low heat for 5 minutes—do not boil. Stir in maple syrup. Strain into a mug. Garnish with an orange slice.
nostalgia.why: Some drinks are less recipes than they are memories. This one smells like every good autumn you've ever had.

connection.name: The Paper Plane
connection.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake vigorously. Strain into a chilled coupe glass. No garnish—it stands alone.
connection.why: Equal parts of everything. Nothing dominates. Like any good relationship, it only works in balance.

strength.name: The Iron Hand
ingredients: Pinch of smoked salt on the rim
strength.instructions: Rim half the glass with smoked salt. Combine mezcal, lime, agave, and bitters in a shaker with ice. Shake hard. Strain into the prepared rocks glass over fresh ice.
strength.why: Mezcal is fire that's been underground—it knows something about quiet power and patience.

source.author: Adapted from the classic mezcal margarita
source.publication: Mezcal: The History, Craft & Cocktails by Emma Janzen

summer.name: The Long Gold
summer.instructions: Combine rum, pineapple juice, lime juice, and orgeat in a shaker with crushed ice. Shake briefly. Pour unstrained into a tall glass. Crown with more crushed ice and a generous bouquet of mint.
summer.why: Summer in a glass, and the kind that stretches out before you—golden, unhurried, half-asleep.

source.author: A riff on the Mai Tai by Trader Vic, 1944

existentialism.name: The Last Word
existentialism.instructions: Shake all ingredients vigorously with ice. Strain into a chilled coupe glass. No garnish needed.
existentialism.why: A hundred-year-old cocktail that refuses to explain itself. Herbal, sweet, sour, strong—all at once, like being alive.

source.author: Detroit Athletic Club, circa 1916
source.publication: Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails by Ted Haigh

distraction.name: The Unplug
distraction.instructions: Muddle basil leaves with simple syrup in a glass. Add cucumber juice, lime juice, and salt. Fill with ice and top with sparkling water. Stir once.
distraction.why: Cool, green, and impossible to rush. A drink that asks you to taste it instead of scroll past it.

courage.name: The Lion's Tail
courage.instructions: Shake all ingredients with ice. Strain into a chilled coupe glass.
courage.why: Allspice dram tastes like bravery smells—warm, a little reckless, and deeply comforting.

wonder.name: The Stargazer
wonder.instructions: Brew butterfly pea flower tea and cool completely. Pour tea over ice in a tall glass. Add vanilla syrup. Slowly pour in tonic water. Squeeze lemon juice on top and watch the color shift from deep blue to violet. Stir gently.
wonder.why: It changes color in front of your eyes. If that doesn't inspire wonder, I'm not sure what will.

source.author: Modern botanical cocktail traditions
source.publication: Zero: A New Approach to Non-Alcoholic Drinks by Grant Achatz

discouragement.name: The Reviver
discouragement.instructions: Rinse a chilled coupe glass with absinthe and discard excess. Shake remaining ingredients with ice. Strain into the prepared glass. Garnish with a lemon twist.
discouragement.why: This is the Corpse Reviver No. 1's softer cousin—designed to bring you back from the edge, gently.

hubris.name: The Icarus
hubris.instructions: Make honey-ginger syrup by simmering equal parts honey and water with sliced ginger for 10 minutes, then strain. Shake tequila, syrup, and lemon juice with ice. Strain into a rocks glass over ice. Dust cayenne on top. Garnish with a lemon wheel.
hubris.why: Sweet, then it stings. The cayenne at the end is the lesson you didn't see coming.

source.author: Adapted from the Gold Rush by T.J. Siegal

grief.name: The Still Hour
grief.instructions: Warm oat milk gently—do not boil. Whisk in honey, turmeric, cinnamon, pepper, and cardamom until smooth and golden. Pour into your most comforting mug.
grief.why: Grief is not a thing to fix with a clever drink. This is just warmth, held between your hands.

source.author: Adapted from Ayurvedic golden milk tradition
source.publication: The Modern Ayurvedic Cookbook by Amrita Sondhi

alienation.name: The Outsider
alienation.instructions: Stir vodka, vermouth, Chartreuse, and olive brine with ice. Strain into a chilled martini glass. Garnish with a cornichon on a pick.
alienation.why: A martini that went wandering and came back changed. The Chartreuse makes it an outsider among its peers.

source.author: A variation on the classic Dirty Martini
source.publication: The PDT Cocktail Book by Jim Meehan

presence.name: The Here & Now
presence.instructions: Make rosemary honey syrup by simmering equal parts honey and water with a rosemary sprig for 5 minutes, then cool and strain. Combine tea, grapefruit juice, and syrup in a glass with ice. Top with sparkling water. Garnish with rosemary.
presence.why: White tea is the most present of teas—barely processed, almost still a leaf. This drink asks you to notice it.

toast.name: Lemony Snicket
toast.instructions: Make simple syrup by simmering equal parts table sugar and water until sugar is dissolved, then cool and strain. Fill a glass with ice cubes. Add gin, lemon juice, and simple syrup, if using. Stir. Top with Thomas Henry Bitter Lemon. Garnish with lemon slice.
toast.why: A drink for when you want to say, “Well, that’s just my luck,” and mean it with affection instead of bitterness.
